new_statements.quote: Stress can be predicted according to the following rules. Primary stress falls on the first syllable and secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word except for the following modifications: (i) a non-initial syllable containing a long vowel receives primary stress. (ii) Words with compound stems have primary stress on the first syllable and secondary stress on the first syllable of each subsequent morpheme unless it is a reduplicated morpheme in which case it also receives primary stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Predictable stress: primary stress on the word-initial syllable by default; if a non-initial syllable has a long vowel, that syllable takes primary stress instead (long vowels are rare, <5% of vocabulary, never word-final or in affixes). Secondary stress on the penultimate syllable. Effectively 'first heavy (long-vowel) syllable, else first syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; in compound stems, secondary stress on the first syllable of each non-initial morpheme (a reduplicated morpheme instead carries primary stress as well).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) non-initial long vowel attracts primary stress; (ii) compound stems and reduplications have their own pattern (primary on first syllable, secondary on first syllable of each later morpheme; reduplicant gets primary). No lexical exceptions mentioned.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the (phonological) word; Keen's words are consonant-initial, vowel-final, minimally disyllabic, commonly 3-4 syllables. No phrase-level discussion. Author refers to her 1972 MA thesis for fuller phonological detail.
new_statements.identity_note: Keen describes the language under the name Yukulta (speakers at Doomadgee/Burketown, Gulf of Carpentaria); she notes (p.192, 1.2.1) that 'Kangkalita' (= Ganggalida) is sometimes cited as an alternative name. Same languoid as Glottolog gang1267 / ISO gcd.

sources.note: Section 2.3 Stress, p.198: stress predictable; primary stress on the first syllable, secondary on the penult; but a non-initial syllable with a long vowel takes primary stress; compounds: primary on first syllable, secondary on first syllable of each later morpheme (reduplicants also primary). Also 2.1.2 p.196: vowels slightly lengthened in stressed syllables, centralised in unstressed; long vowels in <5% of vocabulary, never in final syllable or affix, two-thirds in first syllable.

sources.note: Second-hand metrical re-analysis of Keen 1983 data: 'Main stress in Yukulta falls on the first long vowel (heavy syllable) and, if there are no heavy syllables, on the first vowel. Secondary stress is on the penult if possible'; classifies main stress as QS unbounded (End Rule left), secondary as QI bounded trochaic; examples íta, mákuwa, kúlurùna, úrpalùta, pitíːnta, pukalantíːtya.
